utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Ms. Kravetz, the next witness is ready, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Mr. Adnan Merovci. I just wanted to inform Your Honours that this witness has prepared a one-page Albanian document. It's just a handwritten document for himself which contains dates of events that are referred to in his statement, and he has asked to have this in court with him. I have provided a copy to the Defence and have asked him just to alert us in the event he feels the need to refer to this document he has prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Merovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that's shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Adnan Merovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When were you born and where were you born, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I was born on the 18th of May, 1956, in Vushtrri, in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of electric and technical engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In 1999 where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Are you referring to 1989 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: 1999, the year 1999.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In 1999, I was chief of President Rugova's cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when did you begin to work for Mr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I began to work for him as early as in 1989, at the time when the Democratic League of Kosovo was formed and when Mr. Rugova was elected its chairman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. In May of 1999, and April and March of 2000, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to review this statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the information contained in this statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you also previously testified in this Tribunal in the case of Prosecution versus Milutinovic et al in January of 2007?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review the transcript of your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions that you were asked when you testified in the Milutinovic trial, would you provide the same answers, Mr. Merovci?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I think that in essence by answers would be the same, maybe I would use different words to describe the events, but in essence it would be the same, my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this prior statement -- the statement and the prior testimony, the statement is 65 ter 02588 and the prior -- transcript of the prior testimony 0518, and I ask that those exhibits be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00416, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the transcript of earlier evidence will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P00417, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would ask -- kindly ask for the assistance of the usher, if the witness could be provided a copy of his prior statement and we'll be referring to it in court. While that's being done I'll proceed to read the court summary of this witness's evidence. The witness was the personal secretary of Dr. Ibrahim Rugova, the head of the political party called the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK. He describes the climate of unrest in Kosovo from the early 1980s and the legislative measures introduced by Milosevic in 1989 including certainly constitutional amendments which revoked the autonomous status of Kosovo. The witness describes the discrimination faced by Albanians in their jobs. He speaks about the mounting international pressure for a peaceful solution to the Kosovo crisis. In February and March 1999, the witness participated in the Rambouillet and Paris negotiations on the Kosovo crisis and describes these negotiations. When the NATO bombing began on 24th March, 1999, several prominent Albanians were abducted and killed in Kosovo. Dr. Ibrahim Rugova was placed under house arrest. The witness saw an increase in police and military presence in Pristina. The witness speaks about various meetings he attended with Rugova and the Serb leadership from March 1999 onwards, including meetings with Milosevic, Milutinovic, Sainovic, Ratko Markovic, and Zoran Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like to turn to your statement and ask you about some evidence that you provided there. In paragraph 13 of your statement, you refer to events that took place in Kosovo in 1989 and you say that after the removal of Kosovo's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not an objection, just an explanation. I can see that my learned friend is referring to paragraphs, yet I have a statement that's not divided into paragraphs at all, and it's very difficult to follow. The paragraphs are not marked. Is this the statement of May 1999, March 2000 and April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could give page number, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The version in e-court has the paragraph numbers, so I believe my learned colleague doesn't have the version in e-court. We could -- if -- the version in e-court has -- I don't know if you -- we could follow that. I can also indicate the paragraph, the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Page number would help Mr. Djurdjic, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can try also to provide the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I'm referring to page 4, and this is the third paragraph on page 4, which is paragraph 13 and begins with: "After I became involved ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Witness, I was asking you about paragraph 13 of your statement where you refer to the revocation or removal of Kosovo's autonomy in 1989, and you say: "After the abrogation of the autonomy, emergency measures were imposed in Kosovo, effectively martial law ..." is what you say there. Could you very briefly explain how these emergency measures that you refer to in your statement impacted on the daily life of Kosovo Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: With the constitutional amendments imposed violently without the willingness of the population, although the public was against these amendments, the regime in a way implemented this measure to the effect of destructing all the institutions from the lowest to the highest levels, including the education system, health system, police system, legislation, and the society in general in Kosova. This was mainly felt in the education system and health care and in the work of the financial institutions at the time in Kosova in the work of the legislative institutions in Kosova and was manifested with the massive removal of Albanians from their jobs under the pretext of them being Albanians. This can be argumented in different ways, but one of the main arguments is that when Albanians were removed from their works at the time not a single Serb had the same fate. The measures were implemented in the institution where I was employed, in the United Bank of Kosovo. From this bank alone, approximately 260 Albanian employees were dismissed and not a single Serb was dismissed. The education system had the same fate --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I stop you there just so we can clarify part of your answer. You speak about the removal of Albanians from their jobs. By whom were they replaced, these people who were removed from their jobs? You spoke about the massive removal of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When we speak of education institutions, they were not substituted at all. These were Albanian teachers and professors. When we say that the education system was brought down, this means that the teachers and professors as well as teachers and students were forced out of the school buildings. There was no need to substitute them because there were no longer students and professors in the school buildings. In the institution where I was employed, the key positions held by the Albanians at the time were taken away, and Serbs were nominated on those positions. As a result of these measures which affected the economy in Kosova, the bank, as an institution that follows the developments in economy and helps growth, had to go into liquidation. The number of employees was reduced, I mean the number of Albanian, ethnic Albanian employees was reduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You've spoken about employment and also education. Did these measures have any impact on the access to housing and accommodation for Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Taking into consideration the fact that these measures were implemented at a time when Kosova had the growth of a level that it had at the time, there was a system in place to award housing and accommodation to workers. However, once these measures were imposed, this activity was stopped completely vis-a-vis the Albanians. My case is a concrete example. As an engineer and an expert in computer technology in the bank, I was on the list to get an accommodation for my family; but once these measures were implemented, I was denied this right, and instead the apartment was given to a Serb woman who was not there at the time but came and appropriated my apartment. Such cases you could find in other institutions as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your statement, and this is page 5, second paragraph, you speak about the police force, Albanian officers in the police force, and you say that they: "... started to leave the police force in great numbers because of pressures and restrictions put on them by their Serbian colleagues and supervisors." What sort of pressures and restrictions were put on Albanian police officers that forced them to leave their jobs?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When these measures were imposed, this also affected the police system at the time. Most of the employees with the police at the time were Albanians. The police -- Albanian policemen were forced to sign declarations of loyalty towards Serbia and its regime. These Albanian policemen refused to do so; and therefore, they were dismissed from work, under the pretext that they refused to sign their declaration of loyalty towards a regime that was denied by the majority Albanian population in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke a bit earlier about education and you were speaking about teachers being removed from school buildings. Did these measures have any impact on the access of Albanian students to education?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: In the whole territory of Kosova, 99 percent of the education facilities were occupied by Serbs and students, professors, teachers, pupils lost their buildings and their positions. Students were also removed from student hostels. The students were helped by different institutions, including the LDK, which helped them to continue with their education in private facilities, such as apartments, houses, garages, and so on. So Albanians continued to attend schools but not in official school buildings but in private facilities which contained improvised classrooms, built in private homes and basements and garages and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did these special measures remain in force, until when did they remain in force?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The origin of these special measures is at the time of the constitutional amendments, and they were in force until the bombing, NATO bombing, began.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, moving forward a bit in time, in your statement at paragraph 27, you refer to an agreement that was signed between President Milosevic and Dr. Rugova that was facilitated by the Italian Catholic community of St. Egidio. Do you know what was the purpose of this agreement that was signed in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This agreement was a sign of good-will of a non-governmental organisation and a religious community from Roma represented by Vincenzo Paglia. He carried out a shuttle diplomacy between Pristina and Belgrade with the aim of creating or facilitating an agreement that would enable children and teachers to go back to their schools under no conditions. So the aim of this agreement was to facilitate the return of teachers and students to schools. This agreement was signed by Milosevic and by President Rugova. Unfortunately, it was never implemented and failed to yield any success, because at the time the Serb regime did not release these facilities to the Albanians for their use, with the exception of one facility, the Institute of Albanology in Prishtina. The keys to this building were handed over to the Albanian workers in that institute. So with the exception of this facility, no other facility was given back to the Albanians. And that's why I'm saying this agreement was not successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall when the keys of the Institute of Albanology were giving to the workers of that institute and was it handed over, this institute?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but it should be right after the agreement was signed with St. Egidio, but I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving forward to the end of 1998, in paragraph 31, you speak about the -- an agreement that was entered into by Milosevic and US Ambassador Richard Holbrooke which set up the KVM and indicated that Mr. Milosevic would withdraw military and police units from Kosovo, and you then say that after this agreement was signed, you and Mr. Rugova travelled around Kosovo with Christopher Hill. Can you tell us what was the purpose of this trip, this trip that you took with Mr. Rugova and Mr. Hill?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The purpose of the touring of the ground with Ambassador Hill was to see the results and the effect of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement which had two important elements contained in it: One, withdrawal of the troops deployed in Kosova; and two, the establishment of the verification mission headed by Mr. William Walker at the time, so that we could see closely whether these two elements were being fulfilled, mainly, the withdrawal of the Serbian forces. We travelled with Ambassador Walker and Mr. Rugova in the direction of Peja. We visited Rahovec, Malisheve, Suhareke, Lipjan, Shtime, and returned to Prishtina. This is the route that we made on that day. I would like to point out that this was a terrain that at the time was home to offensives, Serb offensives. On the way, we saw many burnt houses, destroyed facilities. We saw worried faces about what was going on and about what had befallen on them. From this picture we could draw the conclusion that the agreement, Milosevic-Holbrooke, was not being implemented. On the way, we saw many tanks and other military vehicles in coveted areas on the hills. There were many check-points, so-called check-points, along the road. And while we were travelling, they pretended not to actually carry out their real role but acted kind of sophisticated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying that they acted kind of sophisticated, did not carry out their real role?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Since we were a delegation of high officials, such as Ambassador Hill and President Rugova, these police check-points in certain situations when we would pass by, these would act passively. They wanted to leave with us the impression that they were check-points just for sake of verification of documents, not for anything else. But these were check-points with combined forces, police and military forces. We passed along 15 such check-points during our travel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in the next paragraph, this is paragraph 32, you refer to the deployment of the KVM and you say, "... but the violence continued as before," this is at the bottom of paragraph 32; and you indicate, "Milosevic did not stick to his agreement to withdraw troops, and in fact even more were introduced into Kosovo." Can you tell us what's the source of your information, why you state this?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It is absolutely true, even though an agreement had been signed that time on the withdrawal and reduction of the number of police and military forces of the regime; that was not the case in actual reality. In fact, their number increased. As a political organisation, namely the Democratic League of Kosovo, we received information from all over Kosova on our activists, members of this league, who operated in the context of the Kosova information centre. We had a representative in every village, people who informed us of what was going on, of every movement; and in this case they also counted the number of the actual vehicles, various vehicles, tanks and so on, on the border with Serbia. And within the day they sent this information to the centre for information where we had special commissions which collected information, drew up the statistics, and published them in the informatory -- bulletin which appeared every day in Albanian and in Serbian. So the main source for our information for every data on the increase of the number of Serb forces and their equipment was the activists of the democratic league who were eye-witnesses to every movement that occurred in every village and on -- along the roads to Pristina mainly from the border, Mitrovica, and others places, all the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, are you referring to a specific time-period when this increase of troops took place?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I am referring mainly to the time-frame -- actually, there are two time-frames, one is following the signing of Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, that is a very intensive period; and the next one, the other one, is the period between Rambouillet and Paris Agreements entailing a three-week period during which the Rambouillet Agreement was signed in Paris. Prior to the signing of this agreement in Paris, in Rambouillet the Albanian side signed a kind of oath, namely, that they will sign the agreement in three weeks' time. And during this interim period of three weeks when we were expecting the NATO air-strikes, Serbia introduced large number of troops and equipment. So this is what I mean when I say about these two periods.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the source of your information about this increase of troops between these two periods would be the same ones that you described earlier, this network of activists of your party, if I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Mainly, yes, even though on the grounds there were foreign reporters as well representing various international media outlets who moved about the territory and passed by such information centres, and sometimes they exchanged information and verified the accuracy of the information. But mainly over 90 percent of our information was received from our activists on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you refer to the period between Rambouillet and the Paris Agreements, and I understand from your statement that that was in March 1999, this period between the Rambouillet and Paris Agreements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This is a period at the end of February until 20th of March. This is the period when the Rambouillet Agreement was signed -- or better to say the meeting that was held in Rambouillet, and then the signing of the Paris Agreement signed, which ended on the 19th of March. On the 19th of March, that agreement was concluded, I mean the Paris Agreement. And this period covers end of February/beginning of March. As I said, it's a three-week period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during this three-week period, were you, yourself, able to observe this increase of troops that you were referring to on the ground, or was this only information you received from activists in the LDK?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At the time we are talking about, this three-week period, the arrival of Serb troops from Serbia to Kosova was a matter of day. It was a transparent issue, everybody could see that. Now, the Serbs no longer took pains to cover-up their activities under the guise of expected air-strikes. So they brought their troops in broad daylight. Therefore, the information came to us from the militants on the grounds, but I, myself, was eye-witness sometimes to such things. Sometimes I, myself, went to the ground, maybe during this three-week period I went two or three times to the ground, because I, myself, kind of was cautious in the movements I made, but I too saw such movements and such increase of troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we move a bit forward in time, in para 44 you refer to the period when you arrived from the Paris talks back to Pristina, and you say that: "There were huge numbers of Serb paramilitaries everywhere." Can you explain who these persons were that you're referring to in your statement as Serb paramilitaries? How were they different from soldiers or policemen?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: When we returned from Paris and that was on the 20th of March, it was a Sunday. During the time we entered Blace border post, we saw a lot of vehicles, international observers, who were leaving Kosova. Mainly they were part of the KVM and other non-government organisations, they were all leaving, and we saw them at the border. We were maybe the only ones who were entering Kosova. I'm talking of our return from Paris. On the way to Prishtina, we saw that things had changed a lot in the meantime, in the sense of a greater presence of police and army along the way, that was a huge presence; so much so that in one of the tunnels on the road bordering Macedonia, that is, from the border with Macedonia, Blace to Prishtina, we could see that the army was installing wires for explosives in the tunnels -- in this tunnel. So that was proof for us that things had changed drastically in these three weeks. When we arrived in Prishtina, we saw that the situation was completely different. On the next day, I moved about in the city to see what was going on, and I saw that there was a large number of armed civilians and vehicles without registration plates and people dressed, some with jackets of a military colour, camouflage, or other dressed in black leather jackets and armed. They were in groups, some smaller, some bigger groups. And after some days, these groups started to become active and to roam along the streets of Prishtina, and this I have seen with my own eyes, maltreating people, forcing people to leave their cars, confiscating their cars, beating them. And then I realised that in Grand Hotel there were Arkan's paramilitaries who were stationed there. I passed by that hotel myself, and I saw that. It was written "Albanians and dogs are forbidden to enter this hotel," and people were saying that Arkan's units were stationed there. The groups of people you are asking me about, consisted people that we referred to as paramilitaries because there was no other name for them, who were different from the members of the regular army and police from their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement in paragraph 45 that "these paramilitaries began destroying Albanian-owned businesses." Is this something you saw yourself, you witnessed this, paramilitaries destroying Albanian-owned businesses?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I witnessed two facilities that were destroyed. I went there after I heard of it, but when I went there the event had already taken place some half an hour ago, and I'm talking of out-patient clinic. At the centre of Prishtina, in Dedinje neighbourhood, the name of which was Resonatsa [phoen], and the eye-witnesses told me that some cars without licence plates had arrived and people dressed in multi -- of uniforms, some civilians, some in uniforms, some without uniforms; and they placed some explosive there, and it was blown up. I went there a half an hour later and saw it with my own eyes. Another instance is that, which happened one day after the air-strikes on the 25th of March, and it was the office of President Rugova and my own office which was burned completely with an explosive, blown up. And I'm saying this based on evidence by eye-witnesses, because the office was situated in an -- in the middle of a neighbourhood, so there were many residents living close by. When I say it was a combined group of people, I mean people dressed in uniforms, semi-uniforms, military uniforms, or civilian clothes, as well as people wearing masks dressed in black but without any insignia, without any epaulette, or anything, any symbol, whereby you could identify them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know whether any non-Albanian shops or businesses were destroyed during these days?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, nobody knows that any such non-Albanian shops or businesses were destroyed or burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just going briefly back to something you said earlier about Arkan's men being at the Grand Hotel in Pristina, is this something that you, yourself, saw or did someone tell you about this? Is this something you heard from others or you observed yourself?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: From a distance, as you might know, Hotel Grand is situated at the centre of the city and there is a space, open space around it. I went close by it and saw this inscription with my own eyes. From a distance I could see that groups of people dressed in black and with masks, some others had some bands, headbands, so I saw them with my own eyes from a relative distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is this inscription that you saw with your own eyes that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: There was a kind of inscription. As I said earlier, it was written like this: "Albanians and dogs are forbidden to enter Grand Hotel."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in paragraph 46, you refer to the start of the NATO bombing, the first night and you say -- you refer to the killing of several prominent Albanians; and you refer specifically to Bajram Kelmendi, Agim Hajrizi, and Latif Berisha. These two persons, Agim Hajrizi, and Latif Berisha, where were they killed?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Latif Berisha and Agim Hajrizi were killed in their own homes. Latif Berisha was the chairman of the branch of the Democratic League of Kosovo in Mitrovica, and this intellectual was also a member of the Presidency of this league and one of the closest collaborators of President Rugova. Mr. Berisha was killed in his own home, and as his family members said, he was called to go out by unidentified persons who spoke in Serbian but people who were dressed in camouflage uniforms. And once he answered to their call he was -- once he appeared at the door-step, he was killed on the spot in his house in Mitrovica. Mr. Agim Hajrizi was an outstanding activist mainly dealing with human rights issues. He was killed also in his own home when some armed groups went to his home and asked him to come out and called him by his name. And once he appeared at the door, they killed him in his home in Mitrovica. This happened in the first days of the air-strikes, that is, on the next day -- on the days immediately after the air-strikes started along with great fighter of human rights, the well-known lawyer, Mr. Bajram Kelmendi, who likewise was taken on the night of the air-strikes from his home with both his sons, and as his wife, Mrs. Kelmendi, said, he was taken by uniformed people and was -- she was then informed of their dead bodies found somewhere in the outskirts of Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say in your statement that: "These killings sent a clear message that Albanian leaders were going to be targets of Serb forces ..." Were these killings reported in the news?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, they were reported. Mainly we heard of that from sources or information sources or media in Albanian, various radio stations, Deutsche Welle, Free Europe, Voice of America, that reported such events; but I may say that the purpose of killing them was to strike terror, to misinform the public, that people are being killed with the sole purpose being to deport the Albanians which was the main -- one of the purposes of the regime, to strike fear among the population for them to leave Kosova, the main aim objective being the ethnic cleansing of Kosova from Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 49 of your statement you refer to the mobilisation of Serbs and you say: "All of them were mobilised in some force or other and everything was done in a coordinated manner." What is the source of this information? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: At this time, the time I'm talking of, the communication between the Albanians and the Serbs was minimal. There were, however, instances when they communicated directly or indirectly, sometimes planned meetings. But we lived in the same buildings. Our neighbours were Serbs. I have seen with my own eyes the door of my neighbour or when the door of the building where we lived was opened, and I could see weapons. I saw once the two sons of my neighbour dressed, one in military -- in arm and the other in police uniforms and quite normally they said, We've been mobilised. And they even said, We were forced to join the army; and that there were other instances when friends and acquaintances said this because these were things that we discussed in our Albanian community, namely, that all the Serbs capable of fighting were mobilised and armed. There was not a single Serb family in Kosova that didn't have at least one weapon. This was a fact of life for everyone, and we could prove it with such facts, some of which I already mentioned. And also that they didn't hide the fact that they were armed. They kept their weapons in bars or restaurants. In the same place you could see Albanians and Serbs to have a coffee or something, and the Serbs showed their weapons openly. This was something that everybody knew about, that every capable Serb who has had a name and a last name was also armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did your neighbours tell you who had provided them with these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Even earlier on, now I'm talking of a later period, so to say, but even at a later time the question of arms and arming the civilian Serb population was a continuous process. We saw what was going on as a political party and democratic league. We could see the gradual arming and organised arming of the Serb population. The tractor or the lorry came near the neighbourhood and distributed, quite openly, weapons to them. But when I'm talking of, that was not so necessary because by then, almost everybody was armed, but this process was done in an organised manner. And I asked my neighbours but I didn't ask them, Who gave you the weapons? But they -- the fact that they themselves said, We are being trained, and in various shooting grounds it was known that everything was done by -- in an organised manner by the state institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, just so we are clear on the time-period you're referring to, you refer to seeing a tractor or a lorry come to the neighbourhood and distribute, quite openly, weapons. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: What I said happened some time in 1996/1997, but by this example I wanted to illustrate the process of arming the Serb population which started even earlier and which was intensified during the last months that we are talking about. But the process of acting -- of arming the Serb population started at an earlier time. The concrete example I gave you you happened in Lakrisht [phoen] neighbourhood in Prishtina, which was the neighbourhood that I lived together with my brother and that I was eye-witness to this distribution of weapons. But the time we are talking about, during this time it was -- the arming was done, as I said, in the light of day. It was done everywhere. People exchanged weapons, got weapons, in the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the next paragraph you refer to: "In the period between 24th March when the bombing started and 29th March ..." and you say you drove to Mr. Rugova's house every day at around 11.00. What if anything, what were you able to observe on the streets of Pristina during these days?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This was the time when the air-strikes started in Kosova and in the territory of Serbia in the former Yugoslavia, and during these days, I went to Mr. Rugova's house since I was a close associate of his. We are talking of the time when Prishtina no longer resembles an ordinary city, when armed groups of soldiers, police, paramilitaries, groups of civilians coming with various cars prevailed, mainly without licence plates. From 24th to the 30th/31st time, during which I travelled to and fro, I saw people and cars being deported in the direction of the outskirts of the city; and then based on testimony by various eye-witnesses, these people in an organised manner were sent by buses in the direction of Skopje or Fushe Kosova to train stations from where they were sent to Macedonia. So convoys of people who were guided and sent to these places often by uniformed people wearing masks and dressed in police uniforms. I have seen real cases in a student township so-called then in Prishtina. I saw a convoy of about approximately over 100 people, lined in three, four, walking on foot, and they were led by a group of some people like the ones I mentioned. They were escorted by these groups towards these directions that I mentioned. During this period, I also saw small groups, a family or two families in a group, escorted by a masked person and three other armed civilians who were heading somewhere that I couldn't communicate with them, but I assumed that they were being driven out. But based on facts, this -- before that these people were looted, their homes were looted, they were asked to hand over money or jewellery and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say you saw columns of -- or convoys of people heading in an organised direction in the direction of Fushe Kosova or Kosovo Polje. Do you know what happened to these people once they arrived to Fushe Kosova?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Based on the information we received later, groups of hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Fushe Kosova, were boarded on trains, and deported to Macedonia. The aim was to bring the population to Fushe Kosova and then make the population board the trains and go to Macedonia. So as I said, the aim was to ethnically cleanse Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who provided this information to you, that this is what was happening in Fushe Kosova, Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: We received this kind of information in different ways. For example, through telephone conversations. As just a few days after the air-strikes began, the phones were still working. Later on, they were no longer working. At the place where I was, the phone was working. So this was a communication between myself and people who had left for Macedonia and who recounted their stories. There were families, for example, that were taken or forced to go to Fushe Kosova and then forced to return to their homes. There were different tactics employed, different movements and games with the population. So I received this kind of information from direct conversation with people or on occasions when I would go on the ground and talk to people just to exchange information as to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, moving a bit forward in time, you say that on the -- in paragraph 51: "On the 29th of March, 1999," you "moved into Dr. Rugova's house ..." and you stayed with him until you left Kosovo. And in the next paragraph you talk about an event that took place on the 31st of March when the MUP came to the house of Dr. Rugova and forced their way in. And you say in that paragraph that you had seen them approaching Dr. Rugova's house going from door to door expelling people. Who were these people that you saw these MUP forces expelling?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: These were people dressed in uniforms. I saw them from the window going door to door in that neighbourhood. Rugova's house is in a hilly part of Prishtina, and from his house, you can see the entire neighbourhood. I could clearly see that these were organised groups escorted by two vehicles. Others were going door to door on foot and forcing the residents out and forcing them to walk down towards the centre of the town. I realised quite soon that our turn will come. I told Mr. Rugova that, We will have to go through the same process, I guess. We went to the upper floor of the house and were watching what was going on from the window. After a short time, these cars manned with police- and army-uniformed personnel approached the house. You can imagine Mr. Rugova's gate to the garden is quite strong, then you have the garden, then you have the door to the house. Without informing us, without knocking on the door, they just smashed the gate, this strong gate that I mentioned. They broke down the door to the house on the ground floor. So as I saw that they wanted to brutally enter the house, I ran down the stairs to the ground floor, as I was scared that they might kill someone from my family. We were a large group there. At the time I got downstairs, I raised my hands instinctively. They jumped at me. I just said to him -- to them, Why are you breaking the door? Do you know who lives here? They didn't speak back. They just jumped on me. They exercised force, physical force, on me, as I have described it in my statement. I was trying to talk to them, to tell them where Mr. Rugova was, and then I saw -- I heard one of them communicating with someone, saying, We are where we are supposed to be. We are in the house of Mr. Rugova, the first person who wanted -- asked for NATO to come here. They beat me and held me there for half an hour with my hands raised up. My family was upstairs. On this occasion, about seven or eight uniformed people entered the house. What I recall is that I saw both police and military uniforms. Some of the uniforms were camouflage, some were not. It was a total chaos. Then they decided to call everybody who was upstairs, come downstairs. They didn't allow me to go out and fetch the family downstairs, but they made me call on them. So more than 20 people came down. They kept us there without any explanation at all for some four hours on the lower floor. So this was it is first encounter with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that more than 20 people came down. Who were these 20 people who came downstairs?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Amongst these 20 people was Mr. Rugova with his family, his wife and three children; the sisters of Rugova's wife, so her three sisters with their families, with their husbands; my wife, because I had decided to remain there with the president; and there was also a German journalist who just happened to be there, who had come there to interview Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did these uniformed people remain in Dr. Rugova's house?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The people dressed in uniforms, both in police and military uniforms, remained there for 24 hours until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when we set off for Belgrade. So they remained there the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to a date and the interpreter didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: From the 31st of March, 1999, up until 4th of May, 1999. So during our stay there, while we were there, all the time they would remain there with us for 24 hours a day. After that, we left and I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during these weeks when these uniformed persons were at Dr. Rugova's house, was Dr. Rugova allowed to circulate freely and leave his house when he wished?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: This event was known to the public. Now, from this period of time when you cast an eye on what had happened, you and everyone can draw the conclusion that we were under a full house arrest, Mr. Rugova, his family, myself, my wife, because from the first encounter with them, their behaviour and throughout this period of time which was more than a month, we always wanted to speak to someone and to be allowed to leave Kosova. It was clear to us that we could not stay there, there was no activity to be done there. That's why we wanted to leave Kosova. As we were not allowed to leave and as they restricted our movement, they didn't allow us to use the phone. They didn't allow us to follow the events on television and in the media. They didn't allow us to move from one room to another. I don't know what else this could be described as but a house arrest. There were so-called phantom meetings, fruitless I would say, organised at the time, both with Milosevic and Milutinovic as well as Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, if I may interrupt you there. I want to go over some of these meetings very briefly because they're already described quite extensively in your written evidence and the evidence that's before Their Honours. In paragraph 57, you refer to a meeting that took place on 1st of April with Mr. Milosevic and you and Mr. Rugova, Dr. Rugova, attended. And you indicate that during these meetings you told Mr. Milosevic about houses being burned, attacks on Albanians, and the expulsions. Did you tell Mr. Milosevic, who was responsible for these events that you were describing during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: During this meeting that I joined on its second half, the topic of the meeting was the issue of Albanians leaving Kosova. He was asking who was causing this massive leaving of the Albanians and replied to his answer by saying that it was NATO bombing. And I reacted immediately, replying to him that it was not NATO, but the Albanians were leaving because of the pressure exercised by the military and police forces; and that these groups that are leaving Kosova are not mentioning NATO as a reason for leaving their homes. I mentioned to him two facts, one of them being the following: Albanians are leaving Kosova and going to Montenegro, and Montenegro is being bombed too, then how can you say that they are fleeing from the NATO bombing? How come they are fleeing from NATO bombing to a country that is being bombed too? The second example I gave him is the following: Vojvodina is also being bombed. How come not a single Serb or Hungarian is leaving Vojvodina because of this bombing, they are human beings too and they are scared too. So I gave concrete examples and this example that I gave, of course, agitated him a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your statement, you referred to a figure of persons who had left and you said you told him that almost 600.000 [Realtime transcript read in error, "6.000"] had left Kosovo. What was the source of this information, this number, that you told Milosevic had left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Excuse me, I see an error here on the transcript. The transcript says 6.000. The figure should be 600.000. I received this information from press conferences held by NATO in Brussels and from following the developments on the news bulletins. I would listen to the news sometimes in hiding and sometimes with the people dressed in uniforms because they were too interested to hear what NATO spokesmen had to say about the developments. So this was a main source of information. The other source was a small radio that we had, and on the radio, we would listen to the news from different world radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just very briefly you say in the next paragraph, this is para 58, that at this meeting a joint statement was signed -- a joint press statement was signed between Mr. Milosevic and Dr. Rugova. Do you recall what this statement said, what it was about?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: It was a statement for a press conference, for the press, two or three lines. It contained, this meeting was organised and the outcome, so-called, from this meeting as stated in the letter was that the Kosova problem should be solved with peaceful means. A lot is said about this statement -- actually, the statement was entitled: Information for the press. It was said in this information for the press that there was a meeting between Rugova and Milosevic, and in the following two lines, two sentences, it was said that the situation in Kosova was discussed at this meeting and that the problem of Kosova should be resolved with democratic and peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, moving now to the month -- later on in the month of April you refer in paragraph 62 to 67 to various visits by Nikola Sainovic to Dr. Rugova's house. Can you tell us who was Nikola Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, he was the deputy prime minister of the federal government at the time. He was in charge of the affairs for Kosova and he was main -- one of the main associates of Milosevic for the issue of Kosova at the time. If I'm not mistaken, his official title was deputy prime minister of the federal government or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us about the complaints that you raised at the meeting with Milosevic. Did you ever raise similar complaints with Sainovic during these visits to Dr. Rugova's house?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, all the time, at every possible meeting, contact. We discussed two main topics, one being our concern about what was going on in Kosova and the ethnic cleansing in Kosova; and the second being our repetitive request to be allowed to go abroad, to leave Kosova. So these were the two main topics that we discussed. I will repeat them again. One being our concern about what was going on in Kosova and the ethnic cleansing in Kosova, and the second issue being our release.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Sainovic's reaction when you raised the issue of what was going on in Kosovo and the ethnic cleansing in Kosovo? How did he react to these complaints?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: He mainly tried to blame it on NATO bombing, saying that the people were fleeing because of the NATO air-strikes. In a way, we started to communicate more "socially." We would say to him, How come not a single family, Serb family, is leaving Kosova? And he would just smile and he would add, We are trying to find a solution to this problem. And this was a time when massacres were already committed in Kosova, when hundreds of thousands of people were being deported. So his purpose was to convince us to organise like political life in Kosova, where only Mr. Rugova and myself as his associates were. There was no other associate of Mr. Rugova, no other activist there. It was only the two of us under house arrest in his house. So his aim was to find a solution. He didn't care much about our concerns, about people leaving Kosova, and about what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in your interactions with him, did you get the impression that he was well-informed of the situation on the ground or not?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: He was absolutely well-informed, and, furthermore, he was responsible for what was going on and he ordered many of those things that were committed there and that were going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why do you say he was responsible for what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: From the meetings we had with him and from the meetings attended by Andjelkovic and Milutinovic and other people from the police, you could tell that he had authority, that he was the finger pointing at what had to be done. So from the atmosphere prevailing on those meetings with him, you could see that he had power, he had authorities. President at the time in Serbia and Belgrade was Milosevic, but in Kosova he was orchestrating everything. Even at the meeting with Milosevic, when we asked him, like, You as a president, can you release us today? And he, Milosevic, would just look at Sainovic. From a statement by Mr. Walker, Sainovic is alleged to be behind the massacre in Racek, behind the events in Racek.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe you described that also in your written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move on to a different topic. I don't know if we want to break now and resume five minutes earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I want to move now to a meeting that took place on the 16th of April, 1999, in Belgrade and which was attended by Mr. Milutinovic, Sainovic, Dr. Rugova, and yourself, and this is described at paragraph 68 of your statement. You described this in quite some detail in your written evidence, so I don't want to go into the details of what occurred at the meeting. I just wanted to ask you: Was Dr. Rugova's and your attendance at this meeting voluntary? Did you feel you had a choice of whether to go to this meeting on the 16th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: As I have described in my statement and testified earlier, after the first meeting with Milosevic we became a sort of hostage and under house arrest; and the activity that they people tried to organise and pass as political meeting was against our wish and readiness, but every time we stated that we are not part of the decision-making to meet them. So each time they asked us to meet we said, We are not part of the decision-making, because normally it takes two to make a decision on a meeting. But the situation being what it was, we were subject to various kind of situations. We were kind of faced with a fait accompli. The car was waiting downstairs for us, and we were taken to this meeting. So all these meetings, as I said, were not voluntary. We were kind of forced to attend them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you say here in your statement that journalists were present to photograph and film everything. Based on what you were able to observe from this meeting on the 1st of April and the second meeting on the 16th of April which took place in Belgrade, did you get the impression that the Serb leadership was seriously engaged in trying to reach a peaceful solution to the Kosovo crisis?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I think that this was more a sort of show-up, a media cover-up of the real situation. I think that the protagonist realised that the problem was between the Serb regime and the NATO-imposed conditions. We had already declared at various meetings that the only solution is the fulfilment of the five well-known points posed by NATO which were often repeated during the press conferences of NATO headquarters. So they were also clear that nothing would come out of such meetings, but they simply wanted to attain two things: One, to gain time and hoping that NATO could hold its air-strikes; and secondly, they were deliberately done to discredit Dr. Rugova in the face of the situation, as a man being manipulated, as a man who was unworthy to represent their demands. It was double-edged, I would say, struggle, first to gain time with the international community, and if that was not the case, then to discredit Mr. Rugova in the eyes of the -- his own people as a man in this case who was being manipulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In paragraph 72, you speak about another meeting which took place in April, on the 28th of April, 1999, and this was a meeting that you and Dr. Rugova attended, and you met with President Milutinovic, Sainovic, Markovic, and Andjelkovic. And you say in this paragraph that you told Milutinovic that people were being forced out of their homes and that your own flat had been destroyed and that the MUP had done it. What was the source of your information that the MUP had destroyed your flat?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: During this meeting that took place where they were located with those persons you mentioned being present, among many things we expressed the concern over what was happening in Kosova, demolition of the houses, the expulsion of the people and so on, giving various examples to them. At this time, the police started to take me out around the city for people to see that everything was okay with me, to make believe that everything was okay. So this -- the source of this information was my own personal experience. And second, I went to visit my flat. I had already closed that flat, and I was assured that nothing would happen to it. So when I went there to visit my flat, escorted by the police, I saw that it was destroyed. They too saw it. And I understood that it was demolished and then looted by other groups. This -- we understood this from a neighbour who, when she saw me, she came out in the street, an old woman, and she said to me that masked police were here with their dogs, dogs they, you know, use in their work. And I asked her whether she knew and who they were, and she repeated twice, They were uniformed and masked police with dogs who came to your apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say that the police had taken you out, were escorting you and taking you out around the city, did this happen before this meeting of the 28th of April, 1999, or when approximately did this occur that you went to visit your flat?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, this occurred sometime after the 1st of May, maybe one week after the 1st of May, maybe it was the 7th or 8th -- sorry, after the 1st of April. It must have been the 7th or the 8th of April, whereas the meeting took place three weeks later. During this time, escorted by the police, I was taken to various places -- I visited several places in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was a document signed at this meeting between President Milutinovic and Dr. Rugova, this meeting of the 28th of April I'm speaking about?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: As far as I know, during the time I was present, nothing was signed. After the end of the meeting I left and -- left the office and in the hallway there was a group of reporters and journalists. From what I understood later, also after hearing what the late President Rugova said, then I understood that they had signed a sort of document like a press release. But this happened after I left the meeting place, when I was talking about to the journalists and I was waiting for Mr. Rugova and Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Sainovic to leave their office. During this interim period probably they had signed this letter that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit 00416 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you had a chance -- while that's being brought up, I just wanted to ask you: Have you had a chance to see this document which was signed since -- yes. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I had a chance --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm calling Exhibit 0 -- 65 ter 00416, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I was asking if you had had the opportunity to see this document since 1999?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I saw this document during the time that the late President Rugova testified, as I'm seeing it now, because there was a live relay of the proceedings and it was in 2001 I think when he testified here. And it was then that I saw it and then I understood that it was a document that was signed at the time I spoke earlier, when I left the office. But it was not signed during the time I was present at this meeting, and I didn't know anything then about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise Dr. Rugova's signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And from what I see it is his -- similar to his signature, but I cannot corroborate that it is exactly his -- it is really his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that you -- you didn't witness the signing of this document but that you understood later that a document was signed between these two persons, Milutinovic and Rugova. What did you understand was the purpose of signing this document that we have up on the screen, this joint statement?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: The way I understand it is that this document, this joint statement, was prepared to give the impression that this was to manage the emergency situation and to show that the Serb regime is cooperative with the person that represents the majority in Kosova. But as I said earlier, the purpose for signing such a document was to convince the international community that something is happening in Kosova, something that is called political cooperation, that politics can play a role as it was with the sole purpose being the stopping of the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seek to tender this document. It's 65 ter 00416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, I just have very few questions left with regard to your statement. If we can look at paragraph 76 of the statement you refer to different tactics used by the MUP of propaganda so Albanians would leave Kosovo. And you say that: "In some instances ... they ... distributed pamphlets with UCK insignia and allegedly signed by Dr. Rugova directed to Albanians ..." Did you have the opportunity to see any of these pamphlets that were distributed?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I didn't see them in the act of distributing them, but I saw them in the hallway before the entrance to my flat. I saw such a pamphlet. I took it -- took a copy of it and saw that it was mere propaganda, both in terms of its content and the way it was formulated, general layout of the pamphlet. It contained many errors, and there was a discrepancy between what it said and the insignia and the person who had signed it. On top there was a KLA insignia and then signed below it was signed by Mr. Rugova, when - as you well know - Mr. Rugova led the LDK and the Kosovo Liberation Army was led by other people. This shows that it was a way to strike fear and panic among the population because that -- the text was full of mistakes in Albanian, which show that it was not done by professionals and that the goal was, as I said, to strike panic among the population, to realise their aim of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at the time did Mr. Rugova have any sort of contact with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 00839 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that is up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document we spoke about and this is what I saw then and which was thrown in front of my door with a KLA insignia --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have on my screen this document in Serbian and it seems to me - and if I may ask my assistant to help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It has just come up now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, the second page of this document is in Serbian. They have been uploaded as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I have no in Serbian -- oh, yes, this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If the witness could please have the original displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can see that the document in the original - could we please look at the original - it is written in the Roman script on red paper -- well, that's not the problem. However, this document is a handwritten document, it's written in the Cyrillic script, and I'm not sure at all if this document -- I don't know who wrote it in this manner because this is not the original. I'm unable to tell what the original is. If this is the original, then I can't be reading the original in the Serbian language and in the Cyrillic script. And you can see the insignia of the Kosovo Liberation Army, the UCK. Could the Judges please see what I'm looking at as the translated document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have three forms of it here. Ms. Kravetz, can you explore the issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. What I can also propose to do is -- this exhibit has been uploaded, what we see as the red sheet and the Cyrillic, as one document. What I'm asking about is the original in the red document. I can also show the other one to the witness, but what I'm seeking to tender into evidence is the red document. So we can also just remove the handwritten document if it is -- satisfies my learned colleague. It is the same document, just three versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it may have the same contents, but it's three totally different documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, one of them is the English translation. I can ask the witness about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you could see the document that's up on the screen, and I don't know how it's being displayed on your screen. I'm speaking about a red document. Have you seen this document before? Are you familiar with this document? And if yes, can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes. It is the same document in contents. Its contents are the same. It is written in Cyrillic letters and the left form is in Albanian with a KLA insignia, but it has many mistakes. The pamphlet that I saw, and which I'm saying here that I saw, it is a document with a KLA insignia. On the right is the English translation, which is word for word the same with the Albanian. The content of the Albanian version is the same with the content of the form written in Cyrillic letters. But as I said earlier, it contains mistakes done only for propaganda purposes, not professionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours, if that adequately covers the crux of the issue raised by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness seems to be saying that no one of these documents are one of the ones that he saw at the time. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I will ask him again. That wasn't my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do any of these documents - and I'm just speaking about either the one in Albanian, the red document, or the handwritten one - do either of these look like the document you said you found when you visited your apartment at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I'm repeating. The document that I saw in front of my door is the red one with the KLA emblem in Albanian. The document in the middle of the screen in Serbian, in Cyrillic letters has the same content. I have seen that too, this piece of paper, but it was not distributed in the streets. The one I saw and which I heard other people having seen is the one on the left side written in Albanian with the KLA emblem and the emblem containing Rugova's alleged signature, name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that clarifies then that there's an identification of the red Albanian document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I seem to tender that document into evidence, Your Honour, and ask that it will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree to the admission of the first document and the English translation; but I object to the admission of the Serbian translation, and I would like to have this document translated in the Serbian in the same way in which it has been translated into English. Well, I really don't know who translated this into Serbian in handwriting and in Cyrillic. I can't identify it. I can see some markings there the -- of this Tribunal, but I don't think that the Serbian version should be admitted. We want to have a proper translation, but we fully agree with the admission of the Albanian and the English versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The red KLA document in Albanian will be admitted with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00419, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is no problem, Your Honour. We're -- and we'll obtain a CLSS translation in B/C/S for that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just one final question, Mr. Merovci, regarding paragraph 75 of your statement. You speak about the period when -- after the NATO bombing began and you say that the VJ and the MUP spread out among vacated Albanian homes and they would put up signs on the doors saying "this is a MUP apartment." Was this something you were able to observe yourself at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances, they were obvious. Some flats contained these signs which said: This is under the protection of the police and MUP. And this prevented the people who usually looted vacant houses from doing so. And this was a way used sometimes also by Albanians who, when forced to leave their apartments or houses, put up such signs in order to protect their houses or apartments from possible looters. So sometimes it was used by -- really by the MUP; sometimes it was as a cover-up to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I saw it -- observed it myself during my walks out in the city escorted by the police, which I mentioned earlier; when I went to my own apartment, in the corridor I saw that: This house is under MUP protection. I saw the sign myself. Sometimes I saw a cross and the state emblem. I observed it with my own eyes in my own entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djurdjic, do you have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Merovci. I am Veljko Djurdjic, a member of the Defence team of the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. Together with me is a member of our team, Ms. Marie O'Leary, and the lead counsel, Mr. Dragoljub Djordjevic, is away on official business related to the preparation of our case. Mr. Merovci, I found part of your answer to one question to be striking. It is in relation to P418; namely, you said that when you watched Mr. Rugova's testimony before this Tribunal on TV, that that was the first time you saw this document with his signature. I think that that was in 2002, but I don't want to be making a mistake here. At any rate, it was in the Milosevic case. Well, up until then, didn't you talk to Mr. Rugova, didn't you ask him -- I mean on the 28th of April, I think it was, 1999, did you ask him what happened and how was it possible that you did not hear that this document had been signed then, how come you didn't find out through the media?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: What was your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. If you didn't understand it, I'm going to break it up into several questions. Did you see Mr. Rugova from the 28th of April, 1999, up until his testimony in The Hague in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I ended my activities relating to Mr. Rugova in the beginning of the year 2000. I returned to my everyday activities and my family, and from that time on, I didn't have meetings with Mr. Rugova of this information character. As I remember it, I think that Mr. Rugova testified here in 2001, so it is a time-period when I left my activities there in Mr. Rugova's office and when I no longer communicated with him on such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after you left the office, what were your relations with Mr. Rugova like?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: Excellent relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I am getting the interpretation into Serbian a bit later, so that is -- that is why I do apologise to Your Honours for my own delay because I have to hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you state anything about your cooperation with Rugova previously, after the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: A book was published, "Questions and Answers of Journalist." The book was published without protocols. Journalist had drafted 100 questions for me, and I provided him with 100 answers; so amongst these questions, there were questions about my ten-year long activity and work with Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did this interview lead to any disruption in your relationship and did it lead to and end in your cooperation?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: No, because I withdrew from these activities in late 1999/beginning of 2000. So I ended up or rounded up my work there in February or March 2000, and the book was published later on. So this has nothing to do with my withdrawal from the activities in his office. It was after that I ended my work with him that this book was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. That's not why you left the office. Tell me, your relationship with Mr. Rugova, after this was published did you stop all contacts with him, or rather, did your contacts stop or not?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I had no ambition for politics. After the ten-year long activity with him, I started to withdraw to my private life, private activities. It had nothing to do with our relationship. Mr. Rugova continued with his activity and I continue with my own activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Merovci, could you answer my questions, the ones that I'm putting to you so we could save time, so that we don't waste any time. I didn't ask you about your politics or political activity at all. I asked you whether on account of what was published you stopped all contacts with Rugova? It is my question. It has nothing to do with politics, and I haven't been able to get an answer from you for five minutes already.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN MEROVCI
utterances.text: I'm still waiting for your question. What is your question? If I understood your question correctly - and, Your Honours, what I understood was whether this book that was published affected our relationship - my answer to that question was that that book was published later on, after I had left the office. I did elaborate on this answer so that you could answer the essence of it. So if you ask me a proper and specific question, I will provide you with a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Mr. Merovci, about the joint statement signed by Dr. Rugova and Milan Milutinovic on the 28th of April, 1999. When did you first learn of the existence of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first time I learned of the existence of that document and of that document having been signed was during Mr. Rugova's testimony. In his testimony, this document was also included. I followed his testimony live on television, and that's when I learned that such a document was signed during that interim time when I left the office and I went to see the journalist. It was a matter of minutes. As I dealt with protocol issues, I had to leave the office before the president to see the journalists to inform them more or less. So it was a matter of minutes later that Mr. Rugova, Mr. Milutinovic, and Sainovic came out to see the journalists. So during the testimony of President Rugova, I realised and learned that this document was signed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to be the case then that you were not told of this document by Dr. Rugova in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not comment on the event. This document we are discussing was spoken of at the press conference, was communicated to the public. And that's why I'm saying that I was not aware of such a document being signed. We did not discuss these issues with Mr. Rugova because, as I said earlier, at the time everything in our eyes was just done in formal terms, just like a cover-up. There was a war for life or death; we chose life. And in a way, we did not want to agitate or irritate those people at the time. And this is the reason why Mr. Rugova signed the document and why we did not discuss these issues any further because they had no value, they were empty. We never discussed these activities with Mr. Rugova because in a way they were non-existent in our eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you know the content of this document from the press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
